description: We are a multidisciplinary team driven by technology, innovation, and space exploration. Our diverse experience in engineering, software development, systems design, and marketing allows us to approach challenges from both technical and creative perspectives. We aim to transform ideas into practical, innovative solutions and create meaningful impact through collaboration, technology, and human-centered design.
summary:
STELLAR Health is an astronaut health monitoring system built by STELLAR LAB for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. On long missions to the Moon or Mars, crews face fluid shifts, muscle and bone loss, poor sleep and isolation, while the nearest doctor is on Earth, often with delays or no signal. Each crew member wears a STELLAR Node: an ESP32 with an ECG chest sensor and a motion sensor that measures heart rate, breathing and movement in real time. The data goes to a cloud database, is analyzed by a Python backend, and is shown in a React web app. The app has a live dashboard, a 3D position view around the capsule, guided training, wellness check-ins and crew views.
Our main difference is evaluation and action. Instead of fixed limits, STELLAR AI learns each astronaut’s own normal and measures how far each new reading moves from it, and for how long. When something changes, it gives an explained alert with a level (self-care, medical officer or Earth), the reason and a clear recommendation, using simple, transparent statistics. A wrist display shows the essentials at a glance. The system is built for autonomy: if a sensor fails, it switches to a backup or simulation and never stops. STELLAR Health is an educational prototype, not a medical device.

Project Details: STELLAR Health

Presentation Video

We have included a short video introducing STELLAR Health and demonstrating the system with real sensors: the chest-mounted node transmitting data, the live application, an explained alert, and wrist mode.

Video: https://www.tiktok.com/t/ZPLwtt8tj/

What does it do, and how does it work?

STELLAR Health is a health-monitoring system designed for astronauts on long-duration missions. It follows the cycle required by the challenge: collect, assess, and act.

Collect. Each crew member wears a STELLAR Node: an ESP32 equipped with an AD8232 ECG sensor on the chest and an MPU6050 motion sensor.

  • It measures heart rate and respiration in real time. Respiration is estimated from the ECG signal itself.
  • It also measures movement and estimates the astronaut’s position relative to the spacecraft.
  • Data is transmitted via Wi-Fi to a cloud database.
  • We are also integrating radiation monitoring, since radiation is one of the greatest risks of spaceflight. This will record each astronaut’s exposure throughout the mission and track their cumulative dose.

Assess. A Python server processes the data. During the first few minutes, STELLAR AI learns each astronaut’s personal baseline—their own normal—and measures how far each new reading deviates from it and for how long.

Act. When a significant change occurs, the system generates an explained alert with three components:

  • The response level: self-care, notify the medical officer, or consult Earth.
  • The reason, written in plain language.
  • A specific recommendation, for example: “Heart rate is 28 bpm above your normal level for 3 minutes, with elevated respiration. Stop and perform 5 minutes of slow breathing.”

Alerts. We are expanding the alert system to include sound notifications and vibration alerts on the wrist display. Radiation alerts are also being added. When exposure increases or the cumulative dose approaches its limit, the astronaut and crew are notified and given a recommended action, such as moving to the spacecraft’s shielded area.

Everything is displayed in a web application:

  • A live dashboard.
  • A 3D view of the astronaut’s position around the spacecraft.
  • Guided exercise with automatic repetition counting.
  • A daily well-being check-in.
  • A commander view for monitoring the entire crew.
  • A Mission Control view for medical teams on Earth.
  • A wrist mode: a smartphone attached to the suit’s sleeve that displays essential information at a glance and can estimate position using steps and a compass.

What benefits does it offer?

  • Earlier detection: It compares each astronaut with their own baseline, allowing it to detect small changes that general thresholds could miss.
  • Clear explanations: It does more than display a number or red warning light. It explains what changed, why it matters, and what to do.
  • Radiation protection: Recording each crew member’s dose will allow the system to issue timely warnings and maintain an exposure history throughout the mission.
  • Greater autonomy: Astronauts can act without waiting for instructions from Earth, which may be more than 20 minutes away when communicating with Mars.
  • Reliability: If a sensor fails, the system automatically switches to a backup source or simulation so that it continues operating.
  • Support for the crew and Earth: The commander can monitor the entire team, while medical personnel receive concise, automated reports.

What is the expected impact?

On missions to the Moon and Mars, crews will need to care for themselves independently for longer periods. STELLAR Health aims to reduce medical risks by detecting fatigue, stress, fever, excessive physical exertion, and radiation exposure at an early stage.

It also seeks to maintain physical health through training that helps prevent muscle and bone loss, while supporting mental health through regular well-being check-ins.

The same concept—“your own normal plus alerts that explain what to do”—can also be used on Earth in remote locations, Antarctic research stations, hazardous workplaces, including environments involving radiation exposure, and for monitoring patients at home.

What tools, languages, hardware, and software did we use?

  • Hardware: ESP32 DevKit, AD8232 ECG sensor with electrodes, MPU6050 accelerometer and gyroscope, and a custom enclosure designed by the team. Wrist mode also uses a smartphone’s accelerometer and compass. A radiation sensor is currently being integrated.
  • Firmware: C++ with Arduino and FreeRTOS. ECG data is sampled at 250 samples per second and movement data at 100 samples per second. Each runs in its own task, and the data is transmitted through HTTPS.
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI.
  • Database: Supabase with PostgreSQL and row-level security. The device can only write data, while read access requires a private server-side key.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, and Vite. Three.js is used for the 3D spacecraft view, and SVG is used for the charts.
  • Deployment: Vercel for the web application and GitHub for source code and team collaboration.
  • Analysis: Transparent, robust statistics—including the median, robust deviation, and z-score—with no “black box.”

How is it creative?

  • Individual baselines instead of fixed thresholds: The system learns what is normal for each astronaut.
  • Alerts that teach: Every alert includes an explanation and a recommended action, with links to relevant exercise or well-being features.
  • Respiration without an additional sensor: Respiratory rate is calculated from the ECG signal.
  • Health and environment combined: The system combines vital signs with each astronaut’s radiation exposure instead of treating them separately.
  • Wrist display: An interface designed specifically for a spacesuit—not simply a smaller web page—with large text, essential information only, and vibration alerts.
  • Multiple position sources with automatic switching: The system can use the node’s sensor, the smartphone, or a simulation.
  • Complete integration: Electronics, firmware, cloud infrastructure, data analysis, and the user interface are combined into a single system built by the team.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Real NASA risks: Isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity, confined environments, and radiation. This is why radiation monitoring is being added.
  • Limited connectivity: The system continues operating and making local decisions even if the connection is lost.
  • Explainability: We selected simple statistical methods that a doctor or astronaut can understand and verify.
  • Data security: Secret keys are never stored on the device or in the webpage, and the device can only write data.
  • Transparency about real and simulated data: The application identifies whether each value comes from the node, smartphone, a manual measurement, or a simulation. Temperature and blood pressure are currently test values, while radiation monitoring is still being integrated.
  • Spacesuit usability: Clear screens, large text, vibration alerts, and critical information displayed first.
  • Technical limitations: Accelerometer-based positioning accumulates errors. The system detects when the estimate becomes unstable and automatically switches sources. A real mission would use radio beacons.
  • Ethics: This is an educational prototype, not a medical device, and this warning is clearly displayed throughout the application.
